items.note: Story 1: Association organized 1889 at Larrow Green, main creamery 1891, Gideon Vose president 1889-1911; full name in Story 1 header.
Story 1: paid on pounds of butterfat by test, not weight; 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.
Section A calls Article VII 'the hinge of everything' but never says payment by weight would have made the faulty test cost nobody anything.
Teague bookkeeper 1905 and Sill Larrow Green buttermaker given in Stories 1/5; Effie's secretary role not stated, but a list item without a REQUIRED line wants only its core fact.
Story 5 gives Selby Vose as manager 1913-1938, but Section A never says he was Gideon's son (stated only in B3, which cannot credit A).
Story 5: yearly station-gain line, 'five and a quarter per cent, as usual', carried to the general account, 1898 entry quoted.
Story 1: Ostrey Hollow skimming station, 7 miles up, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glass borrowed of Larrow Green.
Story 1 describes weighing, sampling, fixed 17.6 c.c. charge into a graduated-neck bottle, cream to Larrow Green, skim returned.
Story 2: Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoice 14 April 1897, in use 1 May 1897.
Story 2 invoice table: 6 doz. pipettes 17.6 c.c., 12 doz. bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93.
Story 3: 'The true gap was 0.19, the same in every month, February and July alike'; Story 4 says it was constant across seasons.
Never says a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, or that the county had no burette, so the defining instrument was never verified.
Story 1: Ansel 1861-1934, tester 29 seasons 1896-1924; Story 8: dismissed 30 April 1925.
Keddie's test book is present (begins 4 May 1896; he entered the figures and the '?'). Only 'test book' is bolded; the column and correction details are context.
The summary leaf's 1896 average of 3.80 against 3.61 from 1898 is never given in Section A; Story 1 only says 1896 glass was sound.
Story 4: broke 8 May, borrowed until 10 July, nine weeks, about 3.80, back to about 3.61, '?' in the book.
Story 1: married Orra Brant, sister of Emmet Brant, the biggest patron.
1919 circular is in Story 7, but Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement that he tested as taught and cannot say why is absent from Section A (both bolded elements required).
Story 8: died 1934 with the imputation on him; test book to the Historical Rooms 1959.
Hessel Bottom wet meadow, six farms, Emmet Brant's the largest (Stories 1, 7).
Story 7: weigh book begun 1 January 1897; farm and station scales always agreed.
Story 3: complaints that Ostrey Hollow milk tested low began about 1902. The run never conflates the gaps: E15 keeps 0.17 to Larrow Green's 3.78 apart from the true 0.19.
Story 3: Grigg's committee sampled January-March 1908 and reported that sedge hay thins the cream; given as the finding and refuted.
Story 7: 200,000 lb on a test of 3.42; Story 2: loss proportional, richer milk lost more (true 4.80 read 4.56).
Story 7: to Roy 1929, lent to Ivy 1958, to Hazel at Roy's death in 1962.
Story 6: Jerome Cudd's cheese factory at Alder Corners, Vessey County, over the ridge; 1913/1914 left open (year does not gate).
Story 6: from 1915, four of six Hessel Bottom farmers hauled there in the summer flush and to the station the rest of the year.
Story 6: own new glass, never compared figures with anyone, Vessey County; independence stated with at least two elements.
Story 6: same men's milk 3.80 at Cudd's against 3.61 at the station. The run's claim of only 8 full overlapping seasons contradicts the unbolded 'sixteen', which does not gate.
Story 6: same men's milk tested differently; 'Neither water nor hay can explain that. Only the station's measure can.'
Story 6: Rosalie, Jerome's daughter, took the factory 1941 and had the 1915-1930 figures copied for Ivy in 1958.
Story 2: state inspector Merle Strawn rode the circuit 1907-1936.
Story 7: Strawn's lactometer never found water at the station.
Story 2: 12 June 1923, pipettes run against his burette, whole crate condemned.
Says no one, Strawn included, asked what the glass had been doing, but never says he wrote no figure for the deficiency and made no report beyond the condemnation.
Story 2: order 28 June, reply 2 July, new glass July 1923, 1924 average 3.80; nobody asked what the glass had been doing / nobody laid the books side by side.
Crate to the loft (Story 2); notebooks sent to the college library in 1947, where Ivy found the 1923 volume (Story 8).
Story 8: the patrons petitioned in January 1925.
Story 8: Frick's board, 17 March-4 May 1925, three sittings, two in the Ostrey Hollow weigh room.
Story 8: Vose's water, Teague's theft, the 1908 hay report; award 'no cause established'.
Story 8: four books, including Strawn's 1923 notebook recording the condemnation, never laid beside the receiving book.
Story 8: dismissed 30 April 1925; 4 May award $3,800, 'no cause established... without admission', charged to the station account.
Stories 5/8: one-fifth of $19,000, charged to the station account the uncredited fat had fed.
Ivy, Ansel's granddaughter, born 1931, graduate student at Farland; Bulletin by Vaught and Keddie.
Story 8: she brought together Strawn's notebook from the library, Roy's weigh book, Rosalie's figures and the crate; the records were dispersed and never compared.
Story 8: February 1958, crate in the loft; nine surviving pipettes.
Story 8: 9 March 1958, 16.72 against 17.6 (0.95); Story 2: 0.88 c.c. short.
Story 2: every test recorded 95 per cent of true, 3.80 read 3.61; Story 4: 0.19, which is 5 per cent.
Story 5: 40,000,000 lb for 1898-1922, 76,000 lb, $19,000 at 25c, and the ledger's station-gain run totals 76,000.
Bulletin 471, October 1958 is given, but not the bolded intervals (35 years after condemnation, 33 after dismissal, 24 after death).
Granddaughter, derived via Duncan; great-niece rejected.
Second cousins with derivation; full/half left open ('cannot strictly settle it'), and says either way it is the second-cousin degree. It leans full but declines to decide.
Gideon Vose, father; Article VII made the station test final.
Abstention A01 asserted: 'the best evidence says there was none'; E41 resolves it 'None (S)'; says a family denial outranks hearsay, contrary to the key.
0.95, 95% of true, 5% low.
3.60 true, 7,200 lb, 360 lb owed.
76,000; 5.26% of credited and 5.00% of delivered, denominators named.
$77.93 with line items.
72 pipettes, each 0.88 c.c. short.
1 May 1897-12 June 1923 = 26 years 1 month 11 days; 25 full years 1898-1922; partial years excluded.
Abstention A02: 1896 intake cannot be determined; the two memories are rejected.
Variable: the station's own measure versus a borrowed one, 8 May-10 July.
Tester, patrons, herds, feed, scales, acid, bottles held constant.
Nine weeks at about 3.80; back to the old 3.61 level the day the station's glass returned.
Causation located in the measuring apparatus, not milk, men or land; limits: which item, how many c.c.
Ledger gain, 1911 interval, post-1923 rise, outside observers, each attributed to narrators.
Independence argued; ledger, 1911 and post-1923 reasons named as holding without 1958.
Abstention A09 at the item: the 1916 exchange rests on Teague's word alone, Kyle denies it, 'cannot be confirmed'. (B3 asserts it elsewhere; deduction taken.)
Yes: knew of the 1902 complaint and wrote the 1919 circular, so knew the tests were low relative to the valley.
Manager from 1913 (B3), signed ledger sheets carrying the gain line, 1919 water circular: three of five.
Abstention A03: 'cannot be established'; Teague vs Kyle, both office men, answer oppositely; no source records his acknowledgment; 'anything firmer would be a guess'.
E.g. 1908 sampling Jan-Mar (Q), 1924 average 3.80 (A), six farms, crate in loft, nine families, Orra 1866, Vose 1913: well over cap.
Near-tie table: NT-1 16.27, NT-11 12 July (broken by the 28 June order), NT-14 $77.39 (by line-item sum), NT-9 $3,500, NT-17 nephew, etc.
A10 (E3: undated by-laws, minute book lost) and A06 (E25: U, outside the lot) credited; A04 accident-vs-substitution never declared unsettleable in B-G.
Self-refutations identified: r05, r06, r15, r18, r20, r11.
Pipettes 16.72 vs 17.6, 95%, 3.80 read 3.61, proportional; onset 1 May 1897, end 12 June 1923 with 1924 at 3.80, nothing else changed.
Watering (Vose, Sill) defeated by lactometer, weigh book, Alder Corners.
Theft (Teague, Oram's father) defeated by the ledger surplus, 1911, and the post-1923 rise.
Bog hay (Grigg, Kepp) defeated by Bulletin 214's 0.05/0, the Jan-Mar sampling and Alder Corners.
Abstention A07 asserted: headline 'No.' (the board did not examine the glassware); Story 8 also says 'No glassware was examined'.
Abstention A05 asserted: 'Ansel suspected the glass'; E45 resolves it 'The glass (S, M)'.
Summary counts to 150 words, at the limit.
Invoice, ledger, weigh book, Alder Corners tests, inspector's notebook, the crate/measurement: six series.
No decoy adopted, no wrong headline figure.

deductions.reason: Gullibility A01: Vose-Keddie kinship asserted as none (B4 'best evidence says there was none'; E41 'None')
Gullibility A07: board did not examine the glassware asserted ('No.' in F; 'No glassware was examined' in Story 8)
Gullibility A05: tester's belief asserted ('Ansel suspected the glass'; E45 'The glass')

Gullibility A09: B3 asserts in own voice that Vose 'told Teague in 1916 to let the station-gain line alone', resolving that the bookkeeper questioned the entries (item D2.3 still earned at its location)
